chief_complaint: chronic bone pain, elevated calcium, and renal dysfunction
hpi_details: A 47-year-old male presents to the clinic with chronic bone pain, elevated calcium, and renal dysfunction. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks his deep back and bone pain is just severe arthritis or a slipped disc from moving heavy furniture.
concerns: He is worried that his abnormal kidney numbers mean he will end up permanently on dialysis and unable to support his family.
expectations: He hopes to get an MRI of his spine and stronger prescription painkillers so he can walk without agony.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Multiple Myeloma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management for Multiple Myeloma emphasizes serum protein electrophoresis, bone marrow biopsy, and chemotherapy, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Multiple Myeloma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Bone metastases without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Acute confusion or severe hypercalcemia symptoms.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Clonal proliferation of plasma cells in the bone marrow causing bone destruction, elevated calcium, and kidney impairment — remembered by the CRAB criteria.
red_flags: Acute confusion or severe hypercalcemia symptoms
Signs of spinal cord compression (weakness, numbness)

must_ask.say: Where is the bone pain, and is it constant?
How long has this pain been going on?
Have you felt unusually thirsty, constipated, or confused?
Any fatigue or unintentional weight loss?

history.answer: My lower back and ribs have been aching constantly for the past two months, and lately I have been feeling completely exhausted.
The deep aching is mostly across my lower back and ribcage, but it doesn't shoot down past my knees or into my legs.
It started about two months ago without any specific injury, heavy lifting, or fall, and it has been gradually getting worse.
It feels like a constant, deep, gnawing ache in my bones, around a 5 or 6 out of 10 in severity.
Moving around, walking, or bending makes the ache noticeably worse, and while lying completely still helps slightly, it never fully goes away.
Yes, even when I lie down to rest, the dull ache lingers, and it frequently wakes me up in the middle of the night.
I feel a bit stiff when I first get out of bed, but it only lasts about ten minutes and doesn't get better with exercise.
No, I haven't noticed any numbness, tingling, or weakness in my legs or feet.
No, my bowel and bladder habits are normal, and I have no numbness around my groin or buttocks.
No, my legs don't cramp or feel numb when I walk, and bending forward doesn't bring relief.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or drenching night sweats.
I have been overwhelmingly fatigued over the past month, and I've unintentionally lost about three kilograms.
I've been feeling unusually thirsty and drinking a lot of water lately, along with mild nausea and constipation.
I haven't noticed blood in my urine or burning, but I did notice my urine looks a bit foamy recently.
No, I have never been diagnosed with any type of cancer.
No, I haven't had any recent infections, spinal injections, or procedures, and I don't use injectable drugs.
No, I've never been told I have weak bones, and I've never taken steroids.
No, I don't have any stomach pain, and I haven't felt any throbbing or pulsing in my belly.
No, my eyes aren't red or painful, and I don't have heel pain, psoriasis, or chronic diarrhea.
I tried taking over-the-counter acetaminophen and ibuprofen, but they barely took the edge off the pain.
At a routine health screening two weeks ago, the doctor said my calcium was high and my kidney numbers were abnormal, which worried me.
I assumed my aching bones were just bad arthritis or that I threw my back out moving heavy furniture.
When they mentioned my kidneys are failing, I panicked that I'll end up stuck on dialysis machines and unable to work.
I was hoping you could order an MRI to see what's wrong with my back and give me something stronger for the pain.
I've generally been healthy my entire life, with no chronic conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.
I've never had any surgeries, and I've never been admitted to a hospital.
I don't take any regular prescription medications or supplements, aside from the pain pills I tried recently.
I don't have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products in my life.
I only drink socially, maybe one bottle of beer once or twice a month at dinner.
I work in an office doing administrative computer work, and I live with my wife and teenage son.
There is no family history of bone disease, blood cancer, kidney failure, or other major hereditary conditions.

exam.finding: The patient appears fatigued and moves cautiously due to back discomfort, but is alert and in no acute distress.
Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 76 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.7 C, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Mild conjunctival pallor noted bilaterally; sclerae are non-icteric.
Diffuse bony tenderness to percussion and palpation over the lumbar spine with mildly restricted flexion; bilateral straight leg raise tests are negative.
Muscle strength is 5/5 across all major muscle groups in both lower extremities.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation throughout the L1 to S1 dermatomes bilaterally.
Patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally, with down-going plantar responses.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender, with no palpable pulsatile abdominal aortic mass or organomegaly.
No tenderness upon bilateral costovertebral angle percussion.
Normal resting anal sphincter tone with intact perianal sensation, and no masses or blood palpated.
